name: Marshmallow test
statement: Preschoolers who hold out longer for a bigger treat are said to become more capable adolescents, making an early wait a marker of later success.
meaning: A child is left alone with a treat and a bell. Ring the bell and the experimenter returns at once, and the child gets the small portion. Wait until the experimenter comes back unprompted, and the child gets the larger one. Seconds waited is the measure. The claim that made the task famous is longitudinal rather than experimental: children who waited longer at about four went on to score higher on the SAT and to be rated by their parents as better at coping with frustration. Nothing in the design assigns a child to wait, so the association is between an early behaviour and a later outcome, not between an intervention and its effect.

origin.who: Walter Mischel, Ebbe B. Ebbesen and Antonette Raskoff Zeiss
origin.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
origin.note: Their paper, "Cognitive and attentional mechanisms in delay of gratification", is the version of the waiting task that the later follow-ups traced back to. The paradigm had appeared two years earlier in Mischel and Ebbesen's "Attention in delay of gratification" in the same journal. The long-run claim arrived later, with Mischel, Shoda and Peake in 1988 and Shoda, Mischel and Peake in 1990.

evidence: The individual experiments were small. Mischel and Ebbesen's 1970 study, the earliest of the series, ran 32 children, 8 to each of four conditions, aged 3 years 6 months to 5 years 8 months. That paper places itself at the King Nursery School of Stanford University, while the 1990 follow-up locates the whole series at the Bing School. Shoda, Mischel and Peake describe the waiting experiments as running at Bing over roughly six years, from 1968 to 1974, with 653 children taking part in at least one. Bing served mostly middle-class children of faculty and students in the university community. Rewards were pairs of items varying in desirability, such as one small marshmallow against two, or one pretzel stick against two. Parents were reached by post about a decade later. The first mailing, in 1981 and 1982, went to the 125 parents whose addresses were known and produced 95 respondents, the sample behind the 1988 paper. A second mailing followed in 1984. Of the 653, 103 had not been tested in the standard waiting situation, no address could be found for 114, and materials came back undelivered for another 32. A sample of 185 children ended up with at least one follow-up measure, and parents of 94 reported SAT scores. Mean delay in that sample was 512.8 s, and mean age at the waiting task was 4 years 4 months. The correlations everyone quotes come from one of four conditions, the one in which the rewards sat in view and no coping strategy was suggested. There, preschool delay time correlated .42 with SAT verbal and .57 with SAT quantitative, on 35 children. In the other three conditions every SAT correlation was negative and none was significant. Parent ratings showed the same pattern: 12 of 14 items on the coping questionnaire were significant in the rewards-exposed condition, against 3 of the 42 correlations across the other three. The authors said plainly that even the highest correlations accounted for only about 25% of the variance.

replication.headline: A much larger sample found the achievement association at about half the original size, and controls for background, home and early test scores cut it by two thirds.
replication.detail: Watts, Duncan and Quan used the NICHD Study of Early Child Care and Youth Development, which recruited at birth at 10 sites across the United States. Children took a 7-minute version of the waiting task at 54 months, with the treat visible and no strategies offered, which the authors identify as the condition Shoda and colleagues called diagnostic. The analytic sample was 918, and most analysis focused on the 552 children whose mothers had not completed college, described in the paper as ten times the size of the Shoda sample. For age-15 academic achievement the standardised bivariate coefficient was 0.24 (SE = 0.04, p < .001). Controls for child background, the home environment and the child's own test scores at 24 and 36 months cut it to 0.08 (SE = 0.03, p = .016). Adding cognitive and behavioural measures from the same 54-month visit cut it to 0.05 (SE = 0.03, p = .140). The paper's own summary is that an extra minute waited at four predicted about a tenth of a standard deviation in age-15 achievement, half the size of the original correlations, reduced by two thirds by the controls. Most of the gradient came from waiting at least 20 s: with those controls in place, the three groups who waited longer than 20 s produced coefficients of 0.23, 0.30 and 0.23, which did not differ from one another (p = .752). The behavioural results were weaker still. No association reached significance between delay time and the mother-reported behaviour composite at Grade 1 or at age 15, with or without controls. The reading was disputed in Psychological Science in 2020. Michaelson and Munakata analysed the same data set under a preregistered plan, scoring the test as waiting the full 7 minutes or not, and reported significant bivariate links to three of five adolescent outcomes: academic achievement 0.27, problem behaviour -0.23 and social skills 0.18. Problem behaviour survived adjustment for the preschool level of the same outcome, at -0.18 (p = .01). Delay time together with social support explained 30.2% of the variance in adolescent problem-behaviour intercepts, against 17.1% for delay time together with self-control. Doebel, Michaelson and Munakata argued in a commentary that executive function and the home environment support delay of gratification, so controlling for them strips out the construct rather than a confound. Watts and Duncan replied in the same issue.

study.cite: Watts, T. W., Duncan, G. J., & Quan, H. (2018). Revisiting the Marshmallow Test: A Conceptual Replication Investigating Links Between Early Delay of Gratification and Later Outcomes. Psychological Science, 29(7), 1159-1177.

limits: No confidence interval sits in the field above because the replication reports standard errors rather than intervals, and reconstructing one is not reading one. The two effect sizes are also not on the same scale. Shoda and colleagues report correlations, and their own paper gives a 95% interval of .10 to .66 for the SAT verbal figure and .29 to .76 for the quantitative one, both from 35 children. Watts and colleagues report standardised regression coefficients, so the schema's original field is left empty rather than filled with a number that cannot be compared. The 0.24 printed above is the estimate for the 552 children of mothers without a degree, not for the full analytic sample of 918. The replication's task stopped at 7 minutes, against 15 to 20 in the Stanford studies, and 55% of children reached that ceiling. The ceiling bit hardest where the original sample sat: 68% of children of college-educated mothers hit it, against 45% of the rest, and the authors say the resulting estimates for the higher-education subsample were too imprecise to support strong conclusions. Neither study randomised anything, and Watts and colleagues state that they make no claim about causal impacts. Falk, Kosse and Pinger published a further comment comparing the two studies directly. Sage answers it with a bot challenge rather than a paywall, and neither Crossref nor PubMed carries an abstract, so its argument is not summarised here. A later wave went further out. Sperber, Vandell, Duncan and Watts followed 702 of the same children to age 26 under a preregistered plan and tested nine outcomes. Two showed bivariate associations, educational attainment at r = .17 and body mass index at r = -.17, and both fell to nonsignificance once controls were added. The wider self-control literature is a separate record, and ego depletion is entry no. 2.
misreadings: The 2018 paper is widely filed as a debunking, and its authors are more careful than that. The achievement association was there, in the predicted direction and statistically significant, at roughly half the original size. What the controls removed was the part not already explained by family background and by what the child could do at the time of the test. Their own closing point is narrower than the headlines: an intervention that lifted waiting time without shifting broader cognitive and behavioural capacity would likely do little. The reverse error is to treat the original finding as though it rested on hundreds of children. It rested on 185 children reached by post, of whom 94 supplied SAT scores, and the celebrated correlations come from 35 of them in a single condition at a single university nursery. A third error is to read the task as a pure measure of willpower. Kidd, Palmeri and Aslin gave 28 children aged 3;6 to 5;10 an art activity in which an adult either kept a promise of better supplies or broke it, then ran the waiting task. Mean wait was 3 min 2 s after the broken promise and 12 min 2 s after the kept one. One of 14 children waited the full 15 minutes in the unreliable condition, against 9 of 14 in the reliable one. Michaelson and Munakata found the same thing when the untrustworthiness was merely witnessed rather than suffered. A child who does not wait may be reading the room correctly. Watts and colleagues add a measurement point in the same direction: their waiting measure correlated .37 with a maths subtest and only .22 to .30 with measures of attention, impulsivity and self-control, which is the wrong pattern for a behavioural proxy for self-control.
